advances: The exponential energy-difference kernel supplies one common lower bound for the canonical midpoint cutoff score and the actual-body integral root-hitting score. Its sharp finite-level capacity gives level-sensitive estimates, and finite support gives different explicit corrections for the two scores. The theorem includes the unrestricted averaged hitting inequality, the bounded-number-of-volume-values consequence, the sharper two-volume coefficient, and an actual-body example on which the overlap tends to zero while the normalized hitting score diverges. These are restricted positive results and an obstruction to the overlap route, not a resolution of the unrestricted locked conjecture.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. All new claims are proved by the finite kernel calculation, elementary integration and inequalities, parity counting, and exact verification of the displayed convex bodies. Root-volume concavity and the two depth transfers are used only through the three declared accepted predecessors. No computational certificate is used.
proof:
We first prove the finite-kernel assertion and the two comparisons in (6). For a real parameter \(s\), let \(g_s(u)=e^{-(s-u)/2}\mathbf1_{\{u\le s\}}\). Direct integration gives
\(\int_{\mathbb R}g_s(u)g_t(u)\,du=e^{-|s-t|/2}\). Hence the matrix \(\mathsf H_{ij}=e^{-|\lambda_i-\lambda_j|/2}\) is a Gram matrix in \(L^2(\mathbb R)\). It is positive definite when the levels are distinct. Indeed, a linear combination of the \(g_{\lambda_i}\) which is zero almost everywhere has its last coefficient zero by restriction to \((\lambda_{m-1},\lambda_m)\), then its preceding coefficient zero in the same way, and finally its first coefficient zero on \((\lambda_1-1,\lambda_1)\). For \(m=1\), the one function has squared norm one, so the same conclusion holds.

For \(m\ge2\), put \(\rho_i=e^{-(\lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i)/2}\) and \(d_i=(1-\rho_i)/(1+\rho_i)=\tanh((\lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i)/4)\). Define a positive discrete measure on the listed energies by

\[
\zeta=\frac12(\delta_{\lambda_1}+\delta_{\lambda_m})
+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}d_i
(\delta_{\lambda_i}+\delta_{\lambda_{i+1}}).
\tag{16}
\]

For \(m=1\), define \(\zeta=\delta_{\lambda_1}\). Write \(\zeta_i\) for its mass at \(\lambda_i\) and \(\kappa=\sum_i\zeta_i=1+\sum_i d_i\), with \(\kappa=1\) in the one-level case. We check its potential exactly. Fix \(k\). For a gap \(i<k\), its contribution to the potential at \(\lambda_k\) is

\[
\frac{d_i}{2}(\mathsf H_{ki}+\mathsf H_{k,i+1})
=\frac12(\mathsf H_{k,i+1}-\mathsf H_{ki}),
\]

because \(\mathsf H_{ki}=\rho_i\mathsf H_{k,i+1}\). For a gap \(i\ge k\), its contribution instead equals \((\mathsf H_{ki}-\mathsf H_{k,i+1})/2\). The left gaps sum to \((1-\mathsf H_{k1})/2\), the right gaps to \((1-\mathsf H_{km})/2\), and the endpoint masses contribute \((\mathsf H_{k1}+\mathsf H_{km})/2\). Their sum is one, also when one of the gap sums is empty. The one-level case has potential one directly. Thus \(\mathsf H\zeta=\mathbf1\) in vector notation.

For any masses \(\beta_i\), Cauchy-Schwarz in this Gram form gives

\[
\left(\sum_i\beta_i\right)^2
=(\beta^{\mathsf T}\mathsf H\zeta)^2
\le(\beta^{\mathsf T}\mathsf H\beta)
(\zeta^{\mathsf T}\mathsf H\zeta)
=\kappa\,\beta^{\mathsf T}\mathsf H\beta.
\tag{17}
\]

All masses \(\zeta_i\) are positive. Therefore the nonnegative vector \(\beta_i=A\zeta_i/\kappa\) is feasible for (5) and attains equality. This proves the exact minimum, including \(A=0\) and \(m=1\). Positive definiteness also shows uniqueness of the minimizer: equality in the Gram Cauchy-Schwarz inequality forces \(\beta\) to be a scalar multiple of \(\zeta\), with its scalar fixed by the total mass. For repeated levels, grouping their masses changes neither the quadratic expression nor the total mass, so the distinct-level assertion applies after aggregation.

In each parity class apply (17) to the masses \(\sum_{\mathbf I\in D_c:e_{\mathbf I}=\lambda_{c,i}}w_{\mathbf I}\). This yields the first inequality in (6). Weighted Cauchy-Schwarz gives \(\sum_c W_c^2/\kappa_c\ge(\sum_c W_c)^2/\sum_c\kappa_c\), proving its second inequality. To remove the parity restriction, let \(f_c=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D_c}w_{\mathbf I}g_{e_{\mathbf I}}\), with the zero function for an empty class. By the same Gram identity,

\[
\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)=\sum_{c\in\{0,1\}^n}\|f_c\|_2^2,
\qquad
\mathscr S_{\mathrm{all}}(w)
=\left\|\sum_{c\in\{0,1\}^n}f_c\right\|_2^2.
\tag{18}
\]

Pointwise Cauchy-Schwarz, followed by integration, bounds the second expression by \(2^n\) times the first. This proves the final inequality in (6), with ordered pairs and all diagonal terms retained.

We next prove (7). The same-parity hypothesis makes every integer midpoint of two supported endpoints supported. It gives, for \(v\in\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}\),

\[
0\le\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)
=e_{\mathbf J+v}+e_{\mathbf J-v}-2e_{\mathbf J}
\le2(b-e_{\mathbf J}).
\tag{19}
\]

This uses only the two endpoint energy upper bounds and the midpoint hypothesis. In particular it does not require a quadratic energy identity. Write \(\Psi_{\mathbf J}=\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}}\alpha(v)e^{-\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)/2}\). Finite summation of the elementary integral identity for \(e^{-\Delta/2}\), stopping at the upper bound in (19), gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Psi_{\mathbf J}
&=\int_0^{2(b-e_{\mathbf J})}\frac12 e^{-L/2}
B_{\mathbf J}^{\Delta}(L)\,dL
+e^{e_{\mathbf J}-b}
B_{\mathbf J}^{\Delta}(2(b-e_{\mathbf J}))\\
&\le K(w)\left[\int_0^{2(b-e_{\mathbf J})}
\frac12e^{-L/2}(1+L)\,dL
+e^{e_{\mathbf J}-b}(1+2(b-e_{\mathbf J}))\right]\\
&=K(w)(3-2e^{e_{\mathbf J}-b}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{20}
\]

When \(b=e_{\mathbf J}\), the integral is zero and the terminal term is the entire cutoff mass, so (20) also includes this boundary case. In all cases the zero displacement is retained exactly. The bound \(B_{\mathbf J}^{\Delta}(L)\le K(w)(1+L)\) is applied at every cutoff, including the terminal one.

Every ordered same-parity pair \((\mathbf I,\mathbf K)\in D^2\) corresponds bijectively to \((\mathbf J,v)=((\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2,(\mathbf I-\mathbf K)/2)\), with \(\mathbf J\in D\) and \(v\in\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}\). The inverse sends \((\mathbf J,v)\) to \((\mathbf J+v,\mathbf J-v)\). At this pair,

\[
\begin{aligned}
w_{\mathbf J}\alpha(v)e^{-\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)/2}
&=\min(w_{\mathbf I},w_{\mathbf K})\sqrt{w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}}\\
&=w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}
e^{-|e_{\mathbf I}-e_{\mathbf K}|/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{21}
\]

Consequently \(\sum_{\mathbf J\in D}w_{\mathbf J}\Psi_{\mathbf J}=\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)\). Multiply (20) by \(w_{\mathbf J}\) and sum. Since \(w_{\mathbf J}e^{e_{\mathbf J}-b}=e^{-b}\), this yields
\(\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)\le K(w)(3W-2Ne^{-b})=K(w)W(3-2\eta)\).
All denominator factors are positive because \(\eta\le1\). Formula (6) now proves the first two bounds in (7).

For \(u\ge0\), \(\tanh u\le u\), as follows by integrating its derivative \(1/\cosh^2u\le1\) from zero. Thus \(\kappa_c\le1+(\lambda_{c,m_c}-\lambda_{c,1})/4\le1+t/4\), and there are at most \(2^n\) occupied classes. Also every positive weight is between \(e^{-b}\) and \(e^{-e_{\min}}\); summing these inequalities gives \(0<e^{-t}\le\eta\le1\). Hence \(\kappa_{\mathrm{par}}\le2^n(1+t/4)\) and \(3-2\eta\le3-2e^{-t}\), proving the last bound in (7). Since each summand \(\tanh u\) is at most one, \(\kappa_c\le m_c\); this proves the per-parity level consequence. At \(t=0\), \(\eta=1\) and every occupied class has one level, giving the stated zero-range bound.

Attainment in (2) follows either from accepted fact `03f071403cdfc69f` or directly from finiteness: at a fixed center it suffices to test the finitely many values \(\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)\), including zero. Between consecutive such values the numerator is constant and the denominator increases. There are finitely many positive centers.

For (8), positive definiteness makes the quadratic form coercive, so its minimum over the shifted lattice is attained, each finite sublevel set contains finitely many lattice points, and the assumed support is nonempty. Convexity of the quadratic form gives
\(Q_{\mathrm{quad}}((\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2-\mathbf a)\le[Q_{\mathrm{quad}}(\mathbf I-\mathbf a)+Q_{\mathrm{quad}}(\mathbf K-\mathbf a)]/2\).
For same-parity supported endpoints this proves both exact support inclusion of the midpoint and the scalar midpoint weight inequality. The minimum supported energy is \(r_{\mathrm{quad}}\), and the maximum supported energy is at most \(R\), so \(t\le R-r_{\mathrm{quad}}\). The two positive factors \(t+4\) and \(3-2e^{-t}\) are nondecreasing for \(t\ge0\). Substitute this comparison in (7) to obtain (8) and its fixed-range consequence, without a comparison to an untruncated Gaussian law.

Now assume the actual-body hypotheses. We use from accepted fact `793210f8a4be3647` its root-volume inequality: for positive source fibers and positive barycentric coefficients at an integer target, the target has positive volume and its volume is at least the \(d\)-th power of the barycentric mean of the source volume roots. For a same-parity pair this yields
\(w_{(\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2}^{1/d}\ge(w_{\mathbf I}^{1/d}+w_{\mathbf K}^{1/d})/2\ge(w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K})^{1/(2d)}\).
It proves the scalar midpoint hypothesis for the complete actual volume table, including its zeros. Applied to each support in (9), it also proves nonnegativity of every root cost. Since every source root is at least \(e^{-b/d}\), its positive barycentric mean is at least \(e^{-b/d}\), and therefore

\[
0\le L_E\le\log(w_{\mathbf J}/e^{-b})=b-e_{\mathbf J}
\quad(E\in\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}).
\tag{22}
\]

In particular \(m_d(\mathbf J,L)\) is constant for \(L\ge b-e_{\mathbf J}\). The finite families in (9) contain the singleton, and their minima exist. The optimized cutoff at each target can be chosen among their finitely many costs, proving attainment as in accepted fact `7fa5a28fe1ac6893`.

Fix an actual center \(\mathbf J\). For a nonzero \(v\in\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}\), its two distinct endpoints form an affinely independent set with barycentric coefficients \(1/2,1/2\) and relative-interior target \(\mathbf J\). Its root cost is bounded by \(\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)/2\), by the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality for the two roots. For \(v=0\), the corresponding support is the singleton and both costs are zero. Distinct unordered nonzero reflected pairs have disjoint endpoint sets and are disjoint from \(\{\mathbf J\}\): any equality of endpoints implies their displacements differ only by sign. Thus a set which hits all the low-cost supports must pay at least the smaller endpoint weight on each retained unordered pair, and must pay the entire central weight. In oriented notation this proves the valid weaker bound

\[
m_d(\mathbf J,L)\ge\frac12B_{\mathbf J}^{\Delta}(2L)
\quad(L\ge0).
\tag{23}
\]

The factor \(1/2\) counts each nonzero unordered pair once. Its right side assigns only \(w_{\mathbf J}/2\) to zero, which is at most the required singleton charge \(w_{\mathbf J}\). No fractional hitting relaxation is used.

Let \(\mathcal A_{\mathbf J}=\int_0^\infty e^{-L}m_d(\mathbf J,L)\,dL\). This is finite since \(m_d(\mathbf J,L)\le W\). By (22) the tail is constant, and the score definition gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal A_{\mathbf J}
&=\int_0^{b-e_{\mathbf J}}e^{-L}m_d(\mathbf J,L)\,dL
+e^{e_{\mathbf J}-b}m_d(\mathbf J,b-e_{\mathbf J})\\
&\le\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)
\left[\int_0^{b-e_{\mathbf J}}e^{-L}(1+L)\,dL
+e^{e_{\mathbf J}-b}(1+b-e_{\mathbf J})\right]\\
&=\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)(2-e^{e_{\mathbf J}-b}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{24}
\]

This identity and estimate also hold when the upper integration endpoint is zero. On the other hand, (23) and finite summation show

\[
\mathcal A_{\mathbf J}
\ge\frac12\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}}\alpha(v)
\int_{\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)/2}^\infty e^{-L}\,dL
=\frac12\Psi_{\mathbf J}.
\tag{25}
\]

Multiply (24)-(25) by the original \(w_{\mathbf J}\), sum over every positive center, and use (21). The result is
\(\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)/2\le\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)(2W-Ne^{-b})\).
Together with (6), this proves the strengthened first line of (10), as well as the stated stronger overlap coefficient. Since \(2-\eta\le2\), its exact same-parity version implies the second line of (10). This also explains why the hitting denominator differs from the denominator in (20): root hitting uses the cutoff \(\Delta/2\) and exponential density \(e^{-L}\), whereas \(K\) uses cutoff \(\Delta\) and density \(e^{-L/2}/2\).

For the \(k\)-volume consequence, all pairs at the same volume level have kernel value one, and all other terms in \(\mathscr S_{\mathrm{all}}(w)\) are nonnegative. Hence \(\mathscr S_{\mathrm{all}}(w)\ge\sum_{\ell=1}^kW_\ell^2\ge W^2/k\), where the last step is Cauchy-Schwarz. Substitute in (10) to obtain (11). Its level-sensitive refinements are already supplied by (6) and the first line of (10).

To prove (12), for any finite lattice set \(A_0\) define the ordered midpoint count
\(r_{A_0}(\mathbf J)=|\{(\mathbf I,\mathbf K)\in A_0^2:\mathbf I+\mathbf K=2\mathbf J\}|\).
Partitioning the endpoints by parity gives

\[
\sum_{\mathbf J\in\mathbb Z^n}r_{A_0}(\mathbf J)
=\sum_{c\in\{0,1\}^n}|(A_0)_c|^2
\ge2^{-n}|A_0|^2.
\tag{26}
\]

Whenever all the pairs counted at \(\mathbf J\) have root cost at most \(L\) and endpoints of weight at least \(u>0\), the disjoint-pair argument proving (23) gives \(m_d(\mathbf J,L)\ge u r_{A_0}(\mathbf J)/2\), again with only a harmless undercharge on a possible diagonal pair.

If all positive volumes equal \(M\), every integer midpoint of supported endpoints is again supported and all its pair costs are zero. Applying (26) to \(D\) and averaging over its \(|D|\) possible midpoint centers gives a \(\mathbf J\in D\) with \(r_D(\mathbf J)\ge2^{-n}|D|\). Consequently \(\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)\ge2^{-n}W/2\), which implies (12).

It remains to treat two distinct positive values \(M>m>0\), both attained. Let \(A_0=\{\mathbf I:w_{\mathbf I}=M\}\), \(B_0=\{\mathbf I:w_{\mathbf I}=m\}\), \(a=|A_0|>0\), \(b_0=|B_0|>0\), and \(\tau=\log(M/m)>0\). For this two-value argument, abbreviate \(\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)\) by \(\mathcal B\). The root-volume inequality makes every integer midpoint of two elements of \(A_0\) have volume at least \(M\), hence exactly \(M\). Its pair cost is zero. Applying (26) and averaging over \(A_0\) therefore gives
\(\mathcal B\ge Ma/2^{n+1}\).

Every integer midpoint of two elements of \(B_0\) belongs to \(D=A_0\cup B_0\). Its pair root cost is exactly \(\log(w_{\mathbf J}/m)\), which is \(\tau\) at a center in \(A_0\) and zero at a center in \(B_0\). This includes the diagonal case in \(B_0\). Hence the same disjoint-pair bound and the definition of \(\mathcal B\) give

\[
r_{B_0}(\mathbf J)\le
\begin{cases}
2\mathcal B(1+\tau)/m,&\mathbf J\in A_0,\\
2\mathcal B/m,&\mathbf J\in B_0.
\end{cases}
\qquad
\frac{b_0^2}{2^n}
\le\frac{2\mathcal B}{m}\bigl(a(1+\tau)+b_0\bigr).
\tag{27}
\]

The last inequality follows by summing and applying (26); no integer midpoint outside \(D\) contributes. Set \(p=Ma/2^n\), \(q=mb_0/2^n\), and \(\rho=(m/M)(1+\tau)\). Thus \(p+q=2^{-n}W>0\), and the two estimates become

\[
\mathcal B\ge\frac p2,
\qquad
\mathcal B\ge\frac{q^2}{2(q+\rho p)}
\ge\frac{q^2}{2(p+q)}.
\tag{28}
\]

The last step uses \(\rho=(1+\tau)e^{-\tau}\le1\), which follows from \(e^\tau\ge1+\tau\). With \(x=p/(p+q)\in[0,1]\), (28) yields
\(\mathcal B/(2^{-n}W)\ge\tfrac12\max\{x,(1-x)^2\}\).
Let \(x_0=(3-\sqrt5)/2\); it lies in \((0,1)\) and satisfies \((1-x_0)^2=x_0\). If \(x\ge x_0\) the first term is at least \(x_0\); if \(x\le x_0\) the second is at least \(x_0\). Thus the lower bound is at least \(x_0/2=(3-\sqrt5)/4\), proving (12) without restricting \(M/m\).

The depth transfer \(h_{\max}(C)\ge K(w)/12\) is exactly the actual-body assertion of accepted fact `03f071403cdfc69f`. The transfer \(h_{\max}(C)\ge\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)/6\), with attainment and the same actual table and root costs, is the assertion of accepted fact `7fa5a28fe1ac6893`. Choose the center, cutoff, and point supplied for the larger of these two numerical bounds, before any halfspace is chosen. This proves the stated combined lower bound at one point with the predecessors' closed-halfspace conventions, including vertical boundaries carrying positive mixed volume.

It remains to verify the actual-body calibration, including the decay estimate. For every nonempty \(T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the minimum of the coordinate functions \(\min_{i\in T}x_i\) is continuous and concave: for \(0\le s\le1\), each coordinate with index in \(T\) of \((1-s)\mathbf x+s\mathbf z\) is at least \((1-s)\min_{i\in T}x_i+s\min_{i\in T}z_i\). Therefore \(a_n\) in (13) is continuous, concave, and at least one on the cube. The set under its graph and above zero over the convex cube is convex and compact. It contains \((0,1)^n\times(0,1)\), so it is full dimensional. Its projection is exactly \([0,1]^n\), whose lattice points are precisely \(\{0,1\}^n\). At a Boolean point with \(k\) coordinates equal to one, precisely the \(2^k-1\) nonempty subsets of those coordinates have minimum one, and all other subsets have minimum zero. Thus the complete fiber at that point is \([0,2^k]\), and fibers outside the cube are empty. This proves the claimed actual table exactly, including all boundary fibers.

Each Boolean vertex is an extreme point of the cube. More explicitly, if it is a positive convex combination of Boolean vertices, a coordinate equal to zero forces that coordinate to be zero in every participating vertex; a coordinate equal to one forces every participating coordinate to equal one. Thus every participating vertex is the target itself. The only member of \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\) is its singleton. It follows that \(m_1(\mathbf J,L)=w_{\mathbf J}\) at every nonnegative cutoff, and the optimized score is the maximum weight \(2^n\), attained at the all-ones target and cutoff zero. Expanding \((1+2)^n\) gives \(W=3^n\), proving (14).

Under the probabilities \(w_{\mathbf I}/W=\prod_{i=1}^n(2^{I_i}/3)\), the coordinates are independent Bernoulli variables with success probability \(2/3\). Therefore \(|\mathbf X|\) and \(|\mathbf Y|\) are independent copies of a random variable \(Z\) with distribution \(\operatorname{Bin}(n,2/3)\), and
\(\mathcal O(w)=\mathbb E[2^{-|Z-Z'|/2}]\).
We give an elementary uniform bound on its point probabilities. Expanding a finite polynomial and integrating each exponential over \([-\pi,\pi]\) shows, for every integer \(k\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(Z=k)
&=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
e^{-iku}\left(\frac13+\frac23e^{iu}\right)^n\,du\\
&\le\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
\left(1-\frac89\sin^2(u/2)\right)^{n/2}\,du\\
&\le\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
e^{-4nu^2/(9\pi^2)}\,du
\le\frac{3\sqrt\pi}{4\sqrt n}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{29}
\]

For the first inequality take the absolute value of the integral and use
\(|1/3+(2/3)e^{iu}|^2=1-(8/9)\sin^2(u/2)\). For the next, use \(1-v\le e^{-v}\) and \(\sin(|u|/2)\ge|u|/\pi\) for \(|u|\le\pi\); the sine inequality follows from concavity and the chord joining zero to \(\pi/2\). For the last inequality enlarge the interval to the real line and use \(\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-a u^2}\,du=\sqrt{\pi/a}\), obtained by squaring the integral and using polar coordinates. Thus (29) is a proved bound, not an appeal to a binomial asymptotic.

For each integer \(r_0\), independence gives
\(\mathbb P(Z-Z'=r_0)=\sum_k\mathbb P(Z'=k)\mathbb P(Z=k+r_0)\le\max_k\mathbb P(Z=k)\).
Consequently, summing the geometric series,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal O(w)
&=\sum_{r_0\in\mathbb Z}2^{-|r_0|/2}\mathbb P(Z-Z'=r_0)\\
&\le\frac{3\sqrt\pi}{4\sqrt n}
\sum_{r_0\in\mathbb Z}(1/\sqrt2)^{|r_0|}
=\frac{3\sqrt\pi}{4\sqrt n}
\frac{1+1/\sqrt2}{1-1/\sqrt2}
=\frac{3\sqrt\pi(3+2\sqrt2)}{4\sqrt n}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{30}
\]

The overlap is positive since diagonal endpoint pairs have positive probability. Equation (30) proves (15), while (14) gives divergence of the normalized hitting score. Finally, if \(W=0\), all claimed nontrivial constructions have explicitly been restricted away from that case; the zero-score conventions and nonnegativity of depth give the stated trivial conclusion at every point of the assumed nonempty \(S\).
statement:
Let \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), let \(w=(w_{\mathbf I})_{\mathbf I\in\mathbb Z^n}\) be a nonzero, nonnegative, finitely supported table of finite real numbers, and define \(D=\{\mathbf I:w_{\mathbf I}>0\}\), \(W=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}w_{\mathbf I}\), and \(N=|D|\). Assume that whenever \(\mathbf I,\mathbf K\in D\) have the same coordinatewise parity, their integer midpoint satisfies \(w_{(\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2}^2\ge w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}\). No extension of the table away from the lattice is required for the scalar assertions. Put

\[
e_{\mathbf I}=-\log w_{\mathbf I}\quad(\mathbf I\in D),\qquad
e_{\min}=\min_{\mathbf I\in D}e_{\mathbf I},\qquad
b=\max_{\mathbf I\in D}e_{\mathbf I},\qquad
t=b-e_{\min},\qquad
\eta=\frac{Ne^{-b}}W.
\tag{1}
\]

All logarithms are natural. Energies are defined only on \(D\); table entries \(w_{\mathbf I}\) outside \(D\) remain zero. One has \(0<e^{-t}\le\eta\le1\).

Use exactly the scalar score of accepted fact `03f071403cdfc69f`, with its index \(j\) written as \(\mathbf J\). At a fixed \(\mathbf J\in D\), set \(\alpha(v)=\min\{w_{\mathbf J+v},w_{\mathbf J-v}\}\), \(\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}=\{v\in\mathbb Z^n:\alpha(v)>0\}\), and \(\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)=\log(w_{\mathbf J}^2/(w_{\mathbf J+v}w_{\mathbf J-v}))\). For \(L\ge0\), define

\[
B_{\mathbf J}^{\Delta}(L)
=\sum_{\substack{v\in\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}\\\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)\le L}}\alpha(v),
\qquad
K_{\mathbf J}(w)=\max_{L\ge0}\frac{B_{\mathbf J}^{\Delta}(L)}{1+L},
\qquad
K(w)=\max_{\mathbf J\in D}K_{\mathbf J}(w).
\tag{2}
\]

These sums are oriented: both \(v\) and \(-v\) occur, and zero occurs once. The curvatures are finite and nonnegative, and both maxima are attained.

For each occupied parity class \(c\), put \(D_c=\{\mathbf I\in D:\mathbf I\equiv c\pmod2\}\) and \(W_c=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D_c}w_{\mathbf I}\). List the distinct energies in this class as \(\lambda_{c,1}<\cdots<\lambda_{c,m_c}\), and define

\[
\kappa_c=1+\sum_{i=1}^{m_c-1}
\tanh\!\left(\frac{\lambda_{c,i+1}-\lambda_{c,i}}4\right),
\qquad
\kappa_{\mathrm{par}}=\sum_{c:D_c\ne\varnothing}\kappa_c.
\tag{3}
\]

An empty sum in (3) is zero, so a class with one energy has capacity one. Equal energies are aggregated before the list is formed. Define the ordered-pair sums and normalized overlap by

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)
&=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf I,\mathbf K\in D\\\mathbf I\equiv\mathbf K\pmod2}}
w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}e^{-|e_{\mathbf I}-e_{\mathbf K}|/2},\\
\mathscr S_{\mathrm{all}}(w)
&=\sum_{\mathbf I,\mathbf K\in D}
w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}e^{-|e_{\mathbf I}-e_{\mathbf K}|/2},\qquad
\mathcal O(w)=\frac{\mathscr S_{\mathrm{all}}(w)}{W^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]

In particular \(\mathcal O(w)=\mathbb E\exp(-|\log w_{\mathbf X}-\log w_{\mathbf Y}|/2)\) for independent indices with probabilities \(w_{\mathbf I}/W\).

For every integer \(m\ge1\), any distinct real numbers \(\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_m\), and any prescribed mass \(A\ge0\), the exact finite-kernel minimum is

\[
\min_{\substack{\beta_i\ge0\\\sum_i\beta_i=A}}
\sum_{i,j=1}^m\beta_i\beta_j e^{-|\lambda_i-\lambda_j|/2}
=\frac{A^2}{\displaystyle 1+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}
\tanh((\lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i)/4)}.
\tag{5}
\]

Consequently, with exactly the capacities in (3),

\[
\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)
\ge\sum_c\frac{W_c^2}{\kappa_c}
\ge\frac{W^2}{\kappa_{\mathrm{par}}},
\qquad
\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)\ge2^{-n}\mathscr S_{\mathrm{all}}(w).
\tag{6}
\]

The midpoint cutoff score satisfies the finite-support estimate

\[
K(w)\ge
\frac{\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)}{W(3-2\eta)}
\ge\frac{W}{(3-2\eta)\kappa_{\mathrm{par}}}
\ge\frac{4}{(t+4)(3-2e^{-t})}\,2^{-n}W.
\tag{7}
\]

If each occupied parity class has at most \(m\ge1\) distinct energies, then also \(K(w)\ge2^{-n}W/[(3-2\eta)m]\ge2^{-n}W/(3m)\), with no restriction on the energy gaps. If \(t=0\), (7) gives \(K(w)\ge2^{-n}W\).

For the finite Gaussian specialization, let \(Q_{\mathrm{quad}}(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax\), where \(A\) is real symmetric positive definite, let \(\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(R\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(R\ge r_{\mathrm{quad}}:=\min_{\mathbf I\in\mathbb Z^n}Q_{\mathrm{quad}}(\mathbf I-\mathbf a)\). Give the complete table the values \(w_{\mathbf I}=e^{-Q_{\mathrm{quad}}(\mathbf I-\mathbf a)}\) when \(Q_{\mathrm{quad}}(\mathbf I-\mathbf a)\le R\), and zero otherwise, including the exact cutoff boundary among the positive entries. Formula (7) holds for its actual distinct energies and actual \(\eta\), and in particular

\[
K(w)\ge
\frac{4}{(R-r_{\mathrm{quad}}+4)
(3-2e^{-(R-r_{\mathrm{quad}})})}\,2^{-n}W.
\tag{8}
\]

For each fixed \(T\ge0\), (8) gives the coefficient \(4/[(T+4)(3-2e^{-T})]\) whenever \(0\le R-r_{\mathrm{quad}}\le T\). No absolute bound uniform over all excess radii is asserted.

For the integral hitting assertions, suppose the scalar table in (1)-(7) is the actual volume table of an arbitrary convex body: \(d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) is a convex body, \(S=C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\ne\varnothing\), and \(w_{\mathbf I}=\mathcal L^d(C_{\mathbf I})\), where \(C_{\mathbf I}=\{\mathbf y:(\mathbf I,\mathbf y)\in C\}\). Thus the table contains the actual volumes of all integer fibers, with empty and lower-dimensional fibers assigned zero, and \(W=\mathcal H_d(S)>0\). For \(\mathbf p\in S\), let \(h_S(\mathbf p)\) be the infimum of \(\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)\) over closed ambient halfspaces \(H\) containing \(\mathbf p\). These actual tables satisfy the scalar midpoint hypothesis.

Use precisely the root-cost and integral hitting conventions of accepted facts `793210f8a4be3647` and `7fa5a28fe1ac6893`. Namely, put \(a_{\mathbf I}=w_{\mathbf I}^{1/d}\); for \(\mathbf J\in D\), let \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\) consist of the nonempty affinely independent sets \(E\subseteq D\) with \(\mathbf J\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}E\), and use their unique positive barycentric coefficients \(\lambda_{E,\mathbf I}\). Define

\[
\begin{aligned}
L_E&=\log\frac{w_{\mathbf J}}
{(\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{E,\mathbf I}a_{\mathbf I})^d},
\qquad
\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}(L)=\{E\in\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}:L_E\le L\},\\
m_d(\mathbf J,L)
&=\min\left\{\sum_{\mathbf I\in F}w_{\mathbf I}:
F\subseteq D,\ F\cap E\ne\varnothing\text{ for every }E\in\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}(L)\right\},\\
\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)
&=\max_{\mathbf J\in D,\ L\ge0}\frac{m_d(\mathbf J,L)}{1+L}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

The singleton \(\{\mathbf J\}\) has cost zero and is included at every nonnegative cutoff. All hitting charges are the full original weights, independent of barycentric coefficients. The score in (9) is integral hitting and is not identified with \(K(w)\) or with the fractional score \(\mathcal B_d(w)\) of those predecessors.

Every root cost at \(\mathbf J\) lies in \([0,b-e_{\mathbf J}]\). The optimized hitting score is attained and obeys

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)
&\ge\frac{\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)}{2W(2-\eta)}
\ge\frac{W}{2(2-\eta)\kappa_{\mathrm{par}}},\\
\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)
&\ge\frac{\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)}{4W}
\ge\frac14\,2^{-n}W\mathcal O(w).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]

More precisely, the last overlap lower bound can be strengthened by replacing \(1/4\) with \(1/[2(2-\eta)]\). The finite-support correction for hitting is therefore different from the correction \(3-2\eta\) for \(K\).

If there are \(k\ge1\) distinct positive volumes and \(W_1,\ldots,W_k\) are their total masses, then

\[
\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)
\ge\frac{2^{-n}}{4W}\sum_{\ell=1}^kW_\ell^2
\ge\frac1{4k}\,2^{-n}W.
\tag{11}
\]

If there are at most two distinct positive volumes, the sharper estimate is

\[
\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)
\ge\frac{3-\sqrt5}{4}\,2^{-n}W.
\tag{12}
\]

These inequalities concern scores optimized over all supported centers and all nonnegative cutoffs. The accepted depth transfers retain their separate normalizations:
\(h_{\max}(C)\ge\max\{K(w)/12,\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)/6\}\), where \(h_{\max}(C)=\max_{\mathbf p\in S}h_S(\mathbf p)\). The resulting depth lower bound is witnessed by one point before the arbitrary closed ambient halfspace, including vertical halfspaces.

Finally, for every \(n\ge1\), there is an actual body with \(d=1\), complete positive support \(D=\{0,1\}^n\), and \(w_{\mathbf I}=2^{|\mathbf I|}\), where \(|\mathbf I|=\sum_i I_i\) on this support. One explicit body is

\[
C_n=\{(\mathbf x,y):\mathbf x\in[0,1]^n,\ 0\le y\le a_n(\mathbf x)\},
\qquad
a_n(\mathbf x)=1+
\sum_{\varnothing\ne T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}
\min_{i\in T}x_i.
\tag{13}
\]

For this body, all fibers outside the displayed support are empty, and

\[
m_1(\mathbf J,L)=w_{\mathbf J}\quad(\mathbf J\in D,\ L\ge0),
\qquad
\mathcal B_1^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)=2^n,\qquad W=3^n,
\qquad
\frac{\mathcal B_1^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)}{2^{-n}W}=(4/3)^n.
\tag{14}
\]

Nevertheless,

\[
0<\mathcal O(w)
\le\frac{3\sqrt\pi\,(3+2\sqrt2)}{4\sqrt n}
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{15}
\]

Thus a uniform positive lower bound for this overlap fails even on actual bodies whose optimized hitting score is much larger than the target scale. If an actual body has \(W=0\), define both scores as zero as in the predecessors; only the trivial zero depth bound is asserted, and none of the positive-support energies, ratios, or probabilities above is defined in that case.
